10010605.p002.s001.text: Climate change is mostly driven by the increase of atmospheric CO2 concentration.

10010605.p002.s002.text: It leads to an increase in ambient temperature and temperature extremes, as well as to a reduction in water availability (Box 1).

10010605.p002.s003.text: Despite the apparent benefit that an increase of CO2 and ambient temperature might have on the production of plant biomass, climate change severely challenges the plant life cycle, and thus increasingly leads to food insecurity.

10010605.p002.s004.text: Investigating the molecular mechanisms of plant adaptation to climate change is thus a pressing issue.

10010605.p002.s005.text: This was the theme of the EMBO Workshop ‘Molecular responses of plants facing climate change’ in June 2022 in Montpellier, France.

10010605.p002.s006.text: Here, we summarize some key insights presented during the conference on the investigation of molecular mechanisms of plant adaptation to environmental constraints in a changing climate.

10010605.p006.s001.text: Ambient temperatures affect all aspects of growth and development.

10010605.p006.s002.text: Morphological responses to mildly elevated temperatures include the regulation of elongation growth in the shoot and the root.

10010605.p006.s003.text: In the shoot, several thermosensors including phytochrome B perceive temperature and coordinate with PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4).

10010605.p006.s004.text: PIF4 then integrates with the auxin and brassinosteroid signalling pathways for a coherent growth response.

10010605.p006.s005.text: Carolin Delker (University of Halle) discussed how shoot and root responses involve distinct sensing and signalling mechanisms.

10010605.p006.s006.text: In nature, however, not only temperatures vary, but also light quality (shading) and water availability.

10010605.p006.s007.text: Jorge Casal (University of Buenos Aires) highlighted the integration of different environmental cues at the level of photoreceptors and downstream signalling pathways to appropriately gauge complex environments.

10010605.p007.s001.text: The heat stress response allows plants to acclimate to extreme temperatures through the activation of HEAT SHOCK TRANSCRIPTION FACTORs (HSFs), which are transcription factors that induce the expression of chaperones (Heat Shock Proteins, HSPs) and enzymes that produce thermoprotective and reactive oxygen species-scavenging metabolites.

10010605.p007.s002.text: The current view is that HEAT SHOCK TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR A1 (HSFA1) isoforms are maintained in an inactive state in the cytoplasm through complexing with chaperones and rapidly move into the nucleus after heat stress to activate transcription, when the HSPs are recruited away from misfolded proteins.

10010605.p007.s003.text: Phil Wigge (IGZ Großbeeren) presented data that suggest an alternative mode of regulation of at least one HSFA1 isoform by liquid–liquid phase separation.

10010605.p007.s004.text: Intrinsically disordered domains within HSFA1 trigger phase separation at elevated temperatures, similar to what has been described for EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3).

10010605.p007.s005.text: Thus, HSFA1 may directly sense temperature.

10010605.p007.s006.text: Temperature-dependent alternative splicing may constitute a parallel mechanism.

10010605.p007.s007.text: Sotirios Fragkostefanakis (University of Frankfurt) reported on general splicing regulators with a specific role in heat stress-dependent alternative splicing, thus illustrating a feedback loop to fine-tune the heat stress response.

10010605.p008.s001.text: A moderate heat stress event can prime a plant and lead to a more efficient response upon recurrent stress after a stress-free interval lasting several days.

10010605.p008.s002.text: This so-called heat stress memory shows complex regulation, including epigenetic modifications, protein stability and stable metabolites.

10010605.p008.s003.text: Isabel Bäurle (University of Potsdam) discussed epigenetic changes involving hyper-methylation of histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) and showed how locus-specific epigenetic editing of H3K4me3 impairs the memory.

10010605.p008.s004.text: Specialized HSF complexes govern these epigenetic modifications.

10010605.p008.s005.text: In contrast, the autophagy cellular degradation machinery negatively impacts heat stress memory by degrading HSPs and other thermoprotective proteins, as Salma Balazadeh (University of Leiden) discussed.

10010605.p008.s006.text: In a parallel pathway the metalloprotease FtsH6 degrades HSP21, thus modulating heat stress memory.

10010605.p008.s007.text: Improving heat stress memory provides an interesting avenue to increase tolerance to heat stress without affecting growth in stress-free conditions.

10010605.p008.s008.text: Improvement of heat stress tolerance may also stem from clever manipulation of the soil microbiome.

10010605.p008.s009.text: Heribert Hirt (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology) presented data showing that desert root endophytes induce thermotolerance by boosting heat stress memory.

10010605.p010.s001.text: Root traits can be targeted to improve water capture in crops and tolerance to water stress based on a good characterization of the stress pattern and soil characteristics of the target area.

10010605.p010.s002.text: Several mechanisms that optimize root development in response to changing soil water content (in time and space) are prime candidates.

10010605.p010.s003.text: Xerobranching, the local inhibition of root branching when the root tip loses contact with wet soil (as in air gaps or dry soil regions), is an abscisic acid (ABA)-dependent adaptive process described in cereals and Arabidopsis.

10010605.p010.s004.text: Malcolm Bennett (University of Nottingham) described how a xerobranching water stress stimulus on a root tip leads to release of ABA from the phloem that induces closure of plasmodesmata in root outer tissues, which prevents the movement of auxin from the epidermis to the pericycle required for lateral root formation.

10010605.p010.s005.text: This model explains how hydraulics controls root architecture via co-transport of phytohormones.

10010605.p010.s006.text: Hydropatterning is another mechanism that regulates the radial positioning of lateral roots, root hairs, or aerenchyma depending on differences in water availability across the circumferential axis of the root to optimize root architecture to local water content.

10010605.p010.s007.text: This adaptive response is ABA-independent but dependent on sumoylation of AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR 7 (ARF7), a key regulator of auxin response during lateral root formation.

10010605.p010.s008.text: José Dinneny (Stanford University) reported that maize varieties are highly diverse for hydropatterning and that hydropatterning was a good predictor of root system depth, a trait associated with better water stress tolerance.

10010605.p011.s001.text: Integrating root architecture and anatomical and physiological properties of tissues is important to understand water dynamics in the root system.

10010605.p011.s002.text: Christophe Maurel (Institute for Plant Sciences of Montpellier) showed by exploiting HydroRoot, a model for root hydraulics, and split root experiments that different maize root types have different hydraulic properties and responses to water stress.

10010605.p011.s003.text: He further reported genetic diversity in maize for root hydraulics.

10010605.p011.s004.text: How root hydraulics relates to plant response to water stress still needs to be evaluated.

10010605.p011.s005.text: Optimizing water acquisition by roots will increase water depletion in the soil and will ultimately have limited impact when available soil water is limited.

10010605.p011.s006.text: Another complementary strategy is to improve water use efficiency, i.e. the amount of carbon fixed per unit water consumed.

10010605.p011.s007.text: Transpiration is regulated by stomatal opening, a process that appeared in the earliest land plants.

10010605.p011.s008.text: Optimizing stomatal movement in response to environmental signals could improve plant water use efficiency and drought tolerance.

10010605.p011.s009.text: Regulation of stomatal closure by ABA and CO2 is mediated by a complex signalling pathway involving several kinases (MPKs, OST1, HT1) and the GHR1 receptor-like pseudokinase, which was described by Hannes Kollist (University of Tartu).

10010605.p011.s010.text: Stomata integrate environmental signals to optimize gas exchange and water loss.

10010605.p011.s011.text: These signalling pathways ultimately lead to the coordinated regulation of different ion transporters localized at the plasma or vacuolar membrane of guard cells as well as aquaporins of the PLASMA MEMBRANE INTRINSIC PROTEIN (PIP) subfamily.

10010605.p011.s012.text: The ability of the plant to restrict its transpiration when the evaporative demand is very high, and therefore when the water cost of carbon fixation is elevated, is a key trait for water use efficiency.

10010605.p011.s013.text: Pablo Affortit (IRD) presented data showing a link between transpiration efficiency and transpiration restriction under high vapour pressure deficit on the one hand and plant hydraulics and root traits (in particular the root/shoot ratio) on the other in African rice, thus linking transpiration regulation to root water uptake.

10010605.p011.s014.text: Interestingly, during drought stress, the photosynthetic apparatus is protected by a feedback control by photorespiration and Anja Krieger-Liszkay (Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell) presented evidence that signals deriving from the plastoquinone pool could regulate root growth.

10010605.p011.s015.text: Altogether, this suggests mechanisms that integrate water stress perception in the photosynthetic tissues with root development and water uptake.

10010605.p011.s016.text: Further work is needed to decipher the regulation of transpiration by plant hydraulics and photosynthesis.

10010605.p013.s001.text: Elevated CO2 concentration (eCO2) promotes the production of biomass, as the current CO2 concentration is a limiting factor for photosynthesis of C3 plants.

10010605.p013.s002.text: As mentioned by Christine Foyer (University of Birmingham), this is a favourable circumstance in a world with a growing population.

10010605.p013.s003.text: However, this CO2 fertilization effect is less than expected due to the acclimation of photosynthesis to eCO2.

10010605.p013.s004.text: Boosting photosynthesis of C3 plants and understanding the mechanisms behind eCO2 acclimation in a CO2-enriched world are therefore main objectives for plant scientists.

10010605.p013.s005.text: Different routes to improve photosynthesis were discussed during this workshop.

10010605.p013.s006.text: One example was presented by Alejandro Perdomo (Lancaster University), who showed that the transcriptional regulation of Rubisco activase can be a way to improve Rubisco efficiency, and thus to increase carbon fixation and yield.

10010605.p013.s007.text: Florian Busch (University of Birmingham) discussed the different limitations of CO2 assimilation, and highlighted that the most relevant targets for improving photosynthesis vary depending on the environment.

10010605.p013.s008.text: Together with Arnold Bloom (UC Davis), Busch stressed the importance of photorespiration, and challenged the view that this metabolic pathway would be a cost for plants compared with the improvement of photosynthesis.

10010605.p014.s001.text: However, the increase in carbon uptake and biomass production will not occur independently of other major metabolic pathways.

10010605.p014.s002.text: This seems especially true considering that photosynthesis might not be the main limiting parameter for growth and yield, in opposition to nutrient and especially nitrogen limitation.

10010605.p014.s003.text: This is reminiscent of an unexpected negative effect of eCO2 on plants.

10010605.p014.s004.text: Indeed, growth under eCO2 leads to a decline in the mineral composition of C3 plants, which might create a serious threat for food and nutritional security at the end of this century.

10010605.p014.s005.text: Different approaches to identify the genetic and molecular mechanisms behind the negative effect of eCO2 on plant nutrient content have been presented.

10010605.p014.s006.text: Antoine Martin (Institute for Plant Sciences of Montpellier) showed that the use of natural genetic variation or the inference of gene networks under simulated future climate notably led to the identification of genes involved in the response of plants to eCO2.

10010605.p014.s007.text: Arnold Bloom presented data showing yield and protein content of several wheat lines over 35 years of cultivation in California.

10010605.p014.s008.text: During this period CO2 increased in the atmosphere, while yield decreased but not protein content, suggesting that plants sacrificed yield to maintain organic N. This also suggests that fast adaptive mechanisms to the changing atmosphere might occur, but remain to be identified.

10010605.p015.s001.text: Plants are also an extraordinary sink of carbon.

10010605.p015.s002.text: The increase of CO2 in the atmosphere may lead to an augmentation in plant biomass, making plants a natural trap for atmospheric CO2 (Box 2).

10010605.p015.s003.text: This was the subject of the keynote given by Joanne Chory (The Salk Institute), who presented data showing how root systems can be improved to capture and store carbon stably in the ground, contributing to the mitigation of climate change.

10010605.p021.s001.text: The complex nature of a changing climate requires plants to be systemically more efficient in dealing with the constraints that have been discussed here individually.

10010605.p021.s002.text: A more integrated view and approach is required, as a plant that is more efficient in dealing with temperature extremes may at the same time be more vulnerable at elevated ambient temperature, under drought stress, or in a CO2-rich environment.

10010605.p021.s003.text: This complexity calls for multi-partner initiatives that have the expertise and the means to tackle systemic aspects, ideally not in model plants, but directly in crop species.

PMC10010605.p002.text: Climate change is mostly driven by the increase of atmospheric CO2 concentration. It leads to an increase in ambient temperature and temperature extremes, as well as to a reduction in water availability (Box 1). Despite the apparent benefit that an increase of CO2 and ambient temperature might have on the production of plant biomass, climate change severely challenges the plant life cycle, and thus increasingly leads to food insecurity. Investigating the molecular mechanisms of plant adaptation to climate change is thus a pressing issue. This was the theme of the EMBO Workshop ‘Molecular responses of plants facing climate change’ in June 2022 in Montpellier, France. Here, we summarize some key insights presented during the conference on the investigation of molecular mechanisms of plant adaptation to environmental constraints in a changing climate.

PMC10010605.p006.text: Ambient temperatures affect all aspects of growth and development. Morphological responses to mildly elevated temperatures include the regulation of elongation growth in the shoot and the root. In the shoot, several thermosensors including phytochrome B perceive temperature and coordinate with PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4). PIF4 then integrates with the auxin and brassinosteroid signalling pathways for a coherent growth response. Carolin Delker (University of Halle) discussed how shoot and root responses involve distinct sensing and signalling mechanisms. In nature, however, not only temperatures vary, but also light quality (shading) and water availability. Jorge Casal (University of Buenos Aires) highlighted the integration of different environmental cues at the level of photoreceptors and downstream signalling pathways to appropriately gauge complex environments.

PMC10010605.p007.text: The heat stress response allows plants to acclimate to extreme temperatures through the activation of HEAT SHOCK TRANSCRIPTION FACTORs (HSFs), which are transcription factors that induce the expression of chaperones (Heat Shock Proteins, HSPs) and enzymes that produce thermoprotective and reactive oxygen species-scavenging metabolites. The current view is that HEAT SHOCK TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR A1 (HSFA1) isoforms are maintained in an inactive state in the cytoplasm through complexing with chaperones and rapidly move into the nucleus after heat stress to activate transcription, when the HSPs are recruited away from misfolded proteins. Phil Wigge (IGZ Großbeeren) presented data that suggest an alternative mode of regulation of at least one HSFA1 isoform by liquid–liquid phase separation. Intrinsically disordered domains within HSFA1 trigger phase separation at elevated temperatures, similar to what has been described for EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3). Thus, HSFA1 may directly sense temperature. Temperature-dependent alternative splicing may constitute a parallel mechanism. Sotirios Fragkostefanakis (University of Frankfurt) reported on general splicing regulators with a specific role in heat stress-dependent alternative splicing, thus illustrating a feedback loop to fine-tune the heat stress response.

PMC10010605.p008.text: A moderate heat stress event can prime a plant and lead to a more efficient response upon recurrent stress after a stress-free interval lasting several days. This so-called heat stress memory shows complex regulation, including epigenetic modifications, protein stability and stable metabolites. Isabel Bäurle (University of Potsdam) discussed epigenetic changes involving hyper-methylation of histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) and showed how locus-specific epigenetic editing of H3K4me3 impairs the memory. Specialized HSF complexes govern these epigenetic modifications. In contrast, the autophagy cellular degradation machinery negatively impacts heat stress memory by degrading HSPs and other thermoprotective proteins, as Salma Balazadeh (University of Leiden) discussed. In a parallel pathway the metalloprotease FtsH6 degrades HSP21, thus modulating heat stress memory. Improving heat stress memory provides an interesting avenue to increase tolerance to heat stress without affecting growth in stress-free conditions. Improvement of heat stress tolerance may also stem from clever manipulation of the soil microbiome. Heribert Hirt (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology) presented data showing that desert root endophytes induce thermotolerance by boosting heat stress memory.

PMC10010605.p010.text: Root traits can be targeted to improve water capture in crops and tolerance to water stress based on a good characterization of the stress pattern and soil characteristics of the target area. Several mechanisms that optimize root development in response to changing soil water content (in time and space) are prime candidates. Xerobranching, the local inhibition of root branching when the root tip loses contact with wet soil (as in air gaps or dry soil regions), is an abscisic acid (ABA)-dependent adaptive process described in cereals and Arabidopsis. Malcolm Bennett (University of Nottingham) described how a xerobranching water stress stimulus on a root tip leads to release of ABA from the phloem that induces closure of plasmodesmata in root outer tissues, which prevents the movement of auxin from the epidermis to the pericycle required for lateral root formation. This model explains how hydraulics controls root architecture via co-transport of phytohormones. Hydropatterning is another mechanism that regulates the radial positioning of lateral roots, root hairs, or aerenchyma depending on differences in water availability across the circumferential axis of the root to optimize root architecture to local water content. This adaptive response is ABA-independent but dependent on sumoylation of AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR 7 (ARF7), a key regulator of auxin response during lateral root formation. José Dinneny (Stanford University) reported that maize varieties are highly diverse for hydropatterning and that hydropatterning was a good predictor of root system depth, a trait associated with better water stress tolerance.

PMC10010605.p011.text: Integrating root architecture and anatomical and physiological properties of tissues is important to understand water dynamics in the root system. Christophe Maurel (Institute for Plant Sciences of Montpellier) showed by exploiting HydroRoot, a model for root hydraulics, and split root experiments that different maize root types have different hydraulic properties and responses to water stress. He further reported genetic diversity in maize for root hydraulics. How root hydraulics relates to plant response to water stress still needs to be evaluated. Optimizing water acquisition by roots will increase water depletion in the soil and will ultimately have limited impact when available soil water is limited. Another complementary strategy is to improve water use efficiency, i.e. the amount of carbon fixed per unit water consumed. Transpiration is regulated by stomatal opening, a process that appeared in the earliest land plants. Optimizing stomatal movement in response to environmental signals could improve plant water use efficiency and drought tolerance. Regulation of stomatal closure by ABA and CO2 is mediated by a complex signalling pathway involving several kinases (MPKs, OST1, HT1) and the GHR1 receptor-like pseudokinase, which was described by Hannes Kollist (University of Tartu). Stomata integrate environmental signals to optimize gas exchange and water loss. These signalling pathways ultimately lead to the coordinated regulation of different ion transporters localized at the plasma or vacuolar membrane of guard cells as well as aquaporins of the PLASMA MEMBRANE INTRINSIC PROTEIN (PIP) subfamily. The ability of the plant to restrict its transpiration when the evaporative demand is very high, and therefore when the water cost of carbon fixation is elevated, is a key trait for water use efficiency. Pablo Affortit (IRD) presented data showing a link between transpiration efficiency and transpiration restriction under high vapour pressure deficit on the one hand and plant hydraulics and root traits (in particular the root/shoot ratio) on the other in African rice, thus linking transpiration regulation to root water uptake. Interestingly, during drought stress, the photosynthetic apparatus is protected by a feedback control by photorespiration and Anja Krieger-Liszkay (Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell) presented evidence that signals deriving from the plastoquinone pool could regulate root growth. Altogether, this suggests mechanisms that integrate water stress perception in the photosynthetic tissues with root development and water uptake. Further work is needed to decipher the regulation of transpiration by plant hydraulics and photosynthesis.

PMC10010605.p013.text: Elevated CO2 concentration (eCO2) promotes the production of biomass, as the current CO2 concentration is a limiting factor for photosynthesis of C3 plants. As mentioned by Christine Foyer (University of Birmingham), this is a favourable circumstance in a world with a growing population. However, this CO2 fertilization effect is less than expected due to the acclimation of photosynthesis to eCO2. Boosting photosynthesis of C3 plants and understanding the mechanisms behind eCO2 acclimation in a CO2-enriched world are therefore main objectives for plant scientists. Different routes to improve photosynthesis were discussed during this workshop. One example was presented by Alejandro Perdomo (Lancaster University), who showed that the transcriptional regulation of Rubisco activase can be a way to improve Rubisco efficiency, and thus to increase carbon fixation and yield. Florian Busch (University of Birmingham) discussed the different limitations of CO2 assimilation, and highlighted that the most relevant targets for improving photosynthesis vary depending on the environment. Together with Arnold Bloom (UC Davis), Busch stressed the importance of photorespiration, and challenged the view that this metabolic pathway would be a cost for plants compared with the improvement of photosynthesis.

PMC10010605.p014.text: However, the increase in carbon uptake and biomass production will not occur independently of other major metabolic pathways. This seems especially true considering that photosynthesis might not be the main limiting parameter for growth and yield, in opposition to nutrient and especially nitrogen limitation. This is reminiscent of an unexpected negative effect of eCO2 on plants. Indeed, growth under eCO2 leads to a decline in the mineral composition of C3 plants, which might create a serious threat for food and nutritional security at the end of this century. Different approaches to identify the genetic and molecular mechanisms behind the negative effect of eCO2 on plant nutrient content have been presented. Antoine Martin (Institute for Plant Sciences of Montpellier) showed that the use of natural genetic variation or the inference of gene networks under simulated future climate notably led to the identification of genes involved in the response of plants to eCO2. Arnold Bloom presented data showing yield and protein content of several wheat lines over 35 years of cultivation in California. During this period CO2 increased in the atmosphere, while yield decreased but not protein content, suggesting that plants sacrificed yield to maintain organic N. This also suggests that fast adaptive mechanisms to the changing atmosphere might occur, but remain to be identified.

PMC10010605.p015.text: Plants are also an extraordinary sink of carbon. The increase of CO2 in the atmosphere may lead to an augmentation in plant biomass, making plants a natural trap for atmospheric CO2 (Box 2). This was the subject of the keynote given by Joanne Chory (The Salk Institute), who presented data showing how root systems can be improved to capture and store carbon stably in the ground, contributing to the mitigation of climate change.

PMC10010605.p021.text: The complex nature of a changing climate requires plants to be systemically more efficient in dealing with the constraints that have been discussed here individually. A more integrated view and approach is required, as a plant that is more efficient in dealing with temperature extremes may at the same time be more vulnerable at elevated ambient temperature, under drought stress, or in a CO2-rich environment. This complexity calls for multi-partner initiatives that have the expertise and the means to tackle systemic aspects, ideally not in model plants, but directly in crop species.
